title: From Doing Everything to Directing Everything

zones.label: Five Tasks, One Pair of Hands
zones.summary: Literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, and manuscript preparation all land on one person, who must reach each one in turn.
facts: The procedural work of research reduces to five recurring tasks: literature search, data analysis, brainstorming, scientific coding, and manuscript preparation (Chapter 1).
The tasks form a pipeline in which the output of each feeds the next, so the whole is only as trustworthy as its weakest stage (Chapter 1).
Chapter 1's illustration: five stages that are each 90 percent likely to be error-free give only about a 59 percent chance that the whole pipeline is clean.
Raising one stage to 99 percent helps little. A verification step at each handoff attacks the product directly, which is why the book spends as much effort on checking as on generating (Chapter 1).

zones.label: The Agent Teams
zones.summary: The same five tasks, now spread across a team: planning agents on the upper tier and execution agents on the lower tier, about 20 and 10 in the book's model.
facts: The book's working model assigns roughly 20 planning agents, which explore, decompose, and specify, and 10 execution agents, which write code, run analyses, and prepare figures (Chapter 1).
The numbers are a design target, not a law. Planning is cheap to parallelize and execution needs closer supervision (Chapter 1).
Planning output is cheap and reversible, so many plans can be produced and you choose. Execution output changes files and costs more attention to check (Chapter 10).
An agent has a goal, tools, a loop, and memory. It takes actions through tools, including actions you did not individually approve (Chapter 1).

zones.label: The Soloist's Bench
zones.summary: One researcher at a cluttered bench at night: an oscilloscope, printed papers, half-written scripts, and cold coffee. Every action in the world is taken by hand.
facts: An assistant answers and waits for you to act. Every action in the world is still taken by you, and you relay each result back by hand (Chapter 1).

An assistant is the right tool for one reviewable transformation, such as explain, rewrite, or convert. It is the wrong tool for many steps whose intermediate results you do not want to relay yourself (Chapter 1).
Electrical engineering raises the stakes of solo work. Numbers carry units, a fabrication run can take months, and a bench measurement cannot be regenerated by a model (Chapter 1).
Doing a task yourself does not make it safe. A script that runs and prints a plausible number can still be wrong, and only your domain knowledge catches it (Chapter 1).

zones.label: The Orchestrator's Bench
zones.summary: The same bench, tidier. The researcher stands with one clipboard and one pen, reviewing a single item that an agent team has prepared.
facts: In the running ADC example the orchestrator reads planning outputs, settles a disagreement between two planners about record length, and approves the procedure (Chapter 1).
Execution agents then run the simulations and compute ENOB. You choose what runs, check what comes back against a test oracle, and sign the result (Chapter 1).
The work has not become easier so much as it has moved, from production to direction and verification (Chapter 1).
The scarcest resource is attention, not typing speed. The useful size of a team is set by how much you can verify, not by how many agents you can launch (Chapter 1).

zones.label: The Crossed-Out Calendar
zones.summary: Doing every step personally spends the researcher's hours on production. Chapter 1 uses a 40-hour manual literature review as an illustrative baseline.
facts: In Chapter 1's illustrative example, a manual literature review of a subtopic takes 40 hours. With an assistant the first pass takes 12 hours, plus 4 hours of verification.
Productivity means validated output per unit of researcher time, so verification counts: 40 / (12 + 4) = 2.5, not the counterfeit 40 / 12 (Chapter 1).
Recovered hours are valuable only if they go to work that needs you, such as reading key papers closely or designing a better experiment (Chapter 1).
The hour counts are illustrative, not measured benchmarks of any tool (Chapter 1).

zones.label: Four Jobs That Stay With You
zones.summary: Directing is not delegating everything. The orchestrator sets direction, supplies domain judgment, resolves conflicts among agents, and decides what is true.
facts: Chapter 1 defines the researcher as orchestrator as the person who sets direction, supplies domain judgment, resolves conflicts among agents, and decides what is true.
Domain judgment example: an agent applied a window function to an already coherent record and lowered the apparent SNDR. Catching it takes knowing a coherent record needs no window (Chapter 1).
When two agents disagree, compare their inputs, settings, and file versions line by line. The disagreement usually sits on one row (Chapter 10).
Delegate tasks that are well specified and checkable. Keep the framing of the question, the choice among approaches, and the final judgment of what is true (Chapter 10).

zones.label: The Thread of Accountability
zones.summary: One maroon thread runs unbroken from the soloist to the orchestrator and ends at a signature. Whoever does the work, the researcher answers for the science.
facts: Accountability for the science stays with the researcher. The orchestrator directs and verifies (Chapter 1).
Every number and every adjective in AI-drafted text is a claim you are about to sign. Chapter 1's draft said 'nearly 10-bit' for a measured 9.26 bits against a 9.5-bit target.
The author list carries accountability that a tool cannot hold, and whether and how to disclose AI assistance is yours to decide (Chapter 1; developed in Chapters 15 and 18).
Review belongs where an action is irreversible, leaves your control, or becomes a reported result (Chapter 1).
A reviewer who has approved fifty correct outputs approves the fifty-first by habit. Review that has become a click is a loop in name only (Chapter 1).

quiz.question: A student must find prior work, analyze measurements, generate design ideas, write simulation scripts, and draft the paper, all personally and one after another. Which region shows this workload?
quiz.explanation: These are the five everyday research tasks of Chapter 1, chained into a pipeline that one person must reach in turn.

quiz.question: Each stage of a five-stage research pipeline has a 90 percent chance of being error-free. Which region shows the chain whose overall chance of a clean result is only about 59 percent?
quiz.explanation: 0.9 multiplied by itself five times is about 0.59, so roughly four runs in ten carry some error to the end. Verification at each handoff is the remedy.

quiz.question: A researcher chats with an assistant, then copies each suggestion into an editor, runs it, and reports the outcome back by hand. Which region shows this way of working?
quiz.explanation: An assistant answers and waits, so every action in the world is taken by you. It is powerful and cheap to supervise, but it does not scale to many steps.

quiz.question: A manual literature review is assumed to take 40 hours. Which region shows the hours of hand work that this baseline stands for in the productivity ratio?
quiz.explanation: The 40 hours are the manual baseline. The honest ratio also counts the 4 hours of verification: 40 / (12 + 4) = 2.5.

quiz.question: Roughly 20 agents explore and specify, and 10 more write code, run analyses, and prepare figures. Which region shows these two groups?
quiz.explanation: Chapter 1's model uses about 20 planning agents and 10 execution agents. The numbers are a design target, not a law.

quiz.question: A researcher reads two planners' outputs, settles a disagreement about record length by reasoning from the converter's bandwidth, and approves the procedure. Which region shows this role?
quiz.explanation: The orchestrator chooses what runs, resolves conflicts among agents, and signs the result. Typing the scripts is no longer the job.

quiz.question: Which region shows the researcher spending attention, the scarcest resource of an agent team, on checking one output at a time instead of typing scripts?
quiz.explanation: The useful size of a team is set by how much you can verify. The work has moved from production to direction and verification.

quiz.question: An agent applied a window function to a record that was already coherent, and the apparent SNDR dropped by a fraction of a bit. Which region shows the kind of job that catches this?
quiz.explanation: Knowing that a coherent record needs no window is domain judgment. It cannot be delegated, and it is one of the jobs that stays with the researcher.

quiz.question: An assistant drafted an abstract that says a converter 'achieves nearly 10-bit resolution', but the measured value was 9.26 bits against a 9.5-bit target. Which region shows the principle that decides who answers for that sentence?
quiz.explanation: Every number and adjective in AI-drafted text is a claim you are about to sign. Accountability does not move to the tool.

quiz.question: A reviewer has approved fifty correct agent outputs in a row and approves the fifty-first without looking. Which region shows the responsibility that this habit puts at risk?
quiz.explanation: Automation bias turns review into a click. The researcher stays accountable on both sides of the divider, so review must stay a real check.
